title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident shows an impersonation scam where fraudsters used personalized messages to pose as NPR Fresh Air staff members and solicit payment from targets. The scammers obtained or generated detailed information about recipients' work and professional backgrounds, then sent emails from lookalike addresses requesting payment for supposed production costs while occasionally requesting social media credentials. The deployment failure occurred at the point of contact: potential guests had no reliable way to verify they were communicating with the actual organization before engaging with the request.

A cybersecurity expert stated that artificial intelligence has made such impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than older mass-fraud attempts. A catch point would have been independent verification by targets, such as calling the organization directly using a known phone number rather than contact information from the email itself. WHYY confirmed the scam is real and is working with law enforcement, though it is not established what technical or procedural measures are being implemented to prevent similar impersonations in the future.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other NPR Fresh Air staff members, sending personalized emails to authors, entertainers and public figures offering interview opportunities. The fraudulent messages include detailed references to targets' work and appear professional, but eventually request payment for production costs ranging around $250. Recipients including Misericordia University history professor Jennifer Black and Emmy-winning comedy writer Bruce Vilanch reported receiving these emails, which sometimes came from addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com and occasionally asked for social media login credentials.

WHYY, NPR and Fresh Air confirmed they are aware of the scam and are working with law enforcement to investigate. The station emphasized that it never charges guests for interviews. Cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege explained that artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than older mass-fraud attempts. Red flags include a major show's host personally handling logistics and any request for payment. WHYY recommends verifying suspicious interview invitations by calling the organization directly rather than responding to the email.
